questions.question: Contoso enables Microsoft Defender for Cloud on a brand-new Azure subscription and buys no paid plan. The CISO sees a Secure Score and a list of recommendations the next morning and asks which capability produced them, and against what benchmark the resources were assessed.
options: Foundational CSPM, which assesses resources against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB) at no extra cost
Defender for Servers Plan 1, which produces the Secure Score for virtual machines only
Defender CSPM, which is free for the first 30 days on every subscription and assesses against PCI DSS
Azure Policy, which generates the Secure Score from policy compliance results
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Foundational CSPM is free and on by default when Defender for Cloud is enabled; it evaluates resources against the MCSB and produces recommendations and the Secure Score. C is wrong: there is no 30-day free Defender CSPM trial, and Defender CSPM is the paid upgrade. D is wrong: Azure Policy enforces configuration, but the Secure Score comes from Defender for Cloud recommendations. B is wrong: Defender for Servers is a paid workload plan, not the source of the score.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Only built-in recommendations from the MCSB affect the secure score."

questions.question: A security engineer remediates three Defender for Cloud recommendations and the Secure Score does not move. Two were marked Preview and one was a custom recommendation the team created. A colleague argues the score only recalculates monthly, and another says the score only counts virtual machines. What explains the unchanged score?
options: The score recalculates monthly, so the change is not visible yet
Only built-in recommendations from the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark affect the Secure Score; Preview and custom recommendations do not
The score only counts recommendations for virtual machines, not other resource types
The score only rises when a workload protection plan such as Defender for Servers is enabled
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Only built-in MCSB recommendations affect the Secure Score, and Preview recommendations are excluded from score calculations; custom recommendations do not count either. A is wrong: controls are recalculated every eight hours, not monthly. C is wrong: the score covers all assessed resource types. D is wrong: the score exists without any paid workload plan.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Recommendations flagged as Preview aren't included in secure score calculations."

questions.question: Fabrikam must demonstrate alignment with PCI DSS and ISO 27001 in addition to its Azure security baseline, and the auditor asks for a single dashboard showing control status for all three frameworks. The team debates whether the MCSB must be replaced. What should they do?
options: Replace the MCSB with PCI DSS, since only one standard can be assigned per subscription
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2, which automatically adds all regulatory standards
Create Azure Policy initiatives named PCI DSS and ISO 27001, because Defender for Cloud cannot assess regulatory frameworks
Assign the PCI DSS and ISO 27001 security standards to the subscription in the Regulatory compliance dashboard; the MCSB remains assigned as the default baseline
questions.explanation: Correct: D. The MCSB is the default standard assigned to every subscription and cannot be removed, and additional standards such as PCI DSS and ISO 27001 can be assigned alongside it; a resource can be evaluated against multiple standards at once. A is wrong: standards are additive, not exclusive. B is wrong: workload plans do not add standards. C is wrong: Defender for Cloud assesses regulatory frameworks through the Regulatory compliance dashboard, with standards backed by Azure Policy initiatives.
questions.source_title: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "When you turn on Defender for Cloud in a subscription, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) standard is applied by default in the subscription."

questions.question: Contoso wants threat detection for its Azure SQL databases (anomalous access, SQL injection attempts) and malware scanning for its storage accounts. The team enables the Defender CSPM plan, expecting both, and nothing is detected. What is the gap, and what provides these detections?
options: Foundational CSPM adds threat detection once the Secure Score exceeds 60 percent, so raise the score first
Microsoft Sentinel is the only service that provides threat detection for databases and storage
Defender for Servers Plan 2 covers SQL and storage threat detection as well as VMs
The Defender CSPM plan is a posture plan, not threat detection; enable the workload protection plans Defender for SQL and Defender for Storage, each scoped to its resource type
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Threat detection comes from workload protection (CWPP) plans enabled per resource type: Defender for SQL for databases and Defender for Storage for storage accounts. Defender CSPM is posture (recommendations, attack paths, governance), not detection. A invents a score threshold. B is wrong: Sentinel ingests alerts from these plans but the detection itself comes from the Defender plans. C is wrong: Defender for Servers protects machines, not SQL or storage.
questions.source_title: SC-500 study guide
questions.source_quote: "Manage security posture by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud."

questions.question: Contoso runs workloads in Azure, an AWS account, a GCP project, and on-premises Windows servers. The CISO wants all of them under one Defender for Cloud posture view and workload protection, without migrating anything. A colleague says Defender for Cloud only supports Azure. What is the correct approach?
options: Connect the AWS account and GCP project with multicloud connectors, and onboard the on-premises servers with Azure Arc so Defender for Servers can protect them
Enable Defender for Cloud on the Azure subscription only; AWS and GCP posture is assessed by their native tools and cannot be shown in Defender for Cloud
Move all workloads into Azure, because Defender for Cloud only supports Azure resources
Install the Microsoft Sentinel agent on every server, which automatically enrolls them in Defender for Cloud
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Defender for Cloud is multicloud: AWS accounts and GCP projects are connected with cloud connectors, and hybrid/on-premises servers are onboarded through Azure Arc so Defender for Servers can protect them. C is wrong: migration is not required. D is wrong: the Sentinel agent does not enroll servers in Defender for Cloud. B is wrong: AWS/GCP posture is shown in the Defender for Cloud dashboard via connectors.
questions.source_title: SC-500 study guide
questions.source_quote: "Manage security posture by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud."

questions.question: A security analyst wants to understand how an attacker could move from an internet-exposed virtual machine to a database holding sensitive data, before any attack happens. The compliance dashboard shows the database control as failed, and the Secure Score is 61 percent. Which capability shows the precomputed chain of exploitable steps, and why do the other two views not answer the question?
options: The Secure Score, which shows the overall percentage of remediated recommendations

Attack path analysis, which shows precomputed paths from an entry point to a critical target; the compliance dashboard shows framework control status, not attack chains, and the Secure Score is an aggregate number
The Regulatory compliance dashboard, which lists the controls that failed for the database
A Defender for Servers security alert, which fires only after an attack is detected
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Attack path analysis uses the cloud security graph to show precomputed exploitable paths from an internet-exposed entry point to a critical asset. The compliance dashboard shows framework control status, not attack chains. Security alerts are reactive detections after an attack begins. The Secure Score is an aggregate posture number, not a path visualisation.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: Contoso has 200 open Defender for Cloud recommendations. The CISO wants each one assigned to a named owner with a due date, with reminders as the deadline approaches, and weekly reporting on overdue items to the security committee. Which feature provides the ownership and deadline mechanism, and what does it not do?
options: Governance rules, which assign recommendations to owners with due dates and reminders; they do not remediate anything themselves
Workflow automation, which automatically remediates every recommendation without an owner
The Secure Score, which assigns owners automatically based on resource tags
Azure Policy remediation tasks, which set deadlines for policy assignments
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Governance rules in Defender for Cloud assign recommendations to owners, set due dates and send reminders; they are the accountability mechanism for posture work. B is wrong: workflow automation triggers Logic Apps on recommendations or alerts but does not assign ownership or deadlines. C is wrong: the Secure Score measures posture; it assigns nothing. D is wrong: Azure Policy remediation tasks fix non-compliant resources but are not the owner/deadline mechanism for Defender recommendations.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: After an acquisition, Contoso suspects the new subsidiary has forgotten subdomains and internet-facing test servers that nobody in IT knows about. The team debates using Defender CSPM, Sentinel, or Network Watcher. Which tool gives an attacker's-eye view of these unknown assets, and how does it start?
options: Azure Network Watcher, which inventories public IP addresses from flow logs
Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (EASM), which starts from seed inputs such as known domains, IP ranges and ASNs and continuously discovers related internet-facing assets
Defender CSPM, which scans the public internet for assets outside the subscription
Microsoft Sentinel, which discovers external assets from the Log Analytics workspace
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Defender EASM is the outside-in capability that discovers internet-facing assets you may not know about, starting from seeds (domains, IP ranges, ASNs) and following connections to build an inventory. C is wrong: Defender CSPM is inside-out and assesses only known resources in connected clouds. D is wrong: Sentinel is a SIEM that ingests logs; it does not crawl the internet for unknown assets. A is wrong: Network Watcher diagnoses Azure networking; it does not discover external attack surface.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: Contoso's Azure VMs need regular vulnerability scanning so missing patches and vulnerable software are reported in Defender for Cloud. The team proposes Defender for Storage, Sentinel analytics rules, or Azure Bastion. Which capability provides this, and where is it configured?
options: Defender for Storage, which scans VM disks for malware
Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules, which scan VMs on a schedule
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, configured through Defender for Servers settings for the VMs
Azure Bastion, which patches VMs during just-in-time sessions
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management (MDVM) provides vulnerability assessment for Azure VMs and is configured in Defender for Servers settings. A is wrong: Defender for Storage protects storage accounts, not VM patch state. B is wrong: Sentinel analytics rules detect threats in ingested logs; they do not scan VMs for vulnerabilities. D is wrong: Azure Bastion provides secure RDP/SSH connectivity, not patching or vulnerability scanning.
questions.source_title: SC-500 study guide
questions.source_quote: "Manage security posture by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud."

questions.question: Contoso's Secure Score is 52 percent. The team remediates a high-severity recommendation that is unique to the PCI DSS standard, with no equivalent control in the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark. The PCI DSS control turns healthy, but the Secure Score does not move. The CISO asks whether the remediation failed. What should the team report?
options: The Secure Score is unchanged, because only built-in Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark recommendations affect it; the PCI DSS control improves only in the Regulatory compliance dashboard
The Secure Score rises only if the team enables the Defender CSPM plan first, which converts compliance fixes into score points
The Secure Score rises but the PCI DSS control stays failed, because compliance data is only refreshed monthly
The remediation failed, because every remediation counts toward the Secure Score
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Only built-in MCSB recommendations affect the Secure Score. A PCI DSS-only recommendation belongs to a different standard's controls, so remediating it improves PCI DSS compliance, not the Secure Score. D confuses the two views. B is wrong: a paid plan does not change which recommendations count toward the score. C is wrong: compliance data is not refreshed monthly, and the control did turn healthy.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Only built-in recommendations from the MCSB affect the secure score."

questions.question: Contoso has only Foundational CSPM enabled (no Defender CSPM plan) and has enabled Defender for Servers Plan 2 on its VMs. The security team opens Defender for Cloud and expects attack path analysis showing how an internet-exposed VM could reach a critical database. A colleague says Plan 2 includes attack paths. What happens?
options: Attack path analysis will be available, because the team enabled Defender for Servers Plan 2, which includes it
Attack path analysis will not be available, because it requires Microsoft Defender XDR incidents to be enabled first
Attack path analysis will not be available, because it requires the paid Defender CSPM plan; Foundational CSPM gives recommendations, Secure Score and inventory, but not attack paths
Attack path analysis will be available, because all posture features are included in the free Foundational CSPM tier
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Attack path analysis and the cloud security explorer's graph queries are Defender CSPM plan features, not part of free Foundational CSPM. Foundational CSPM does give MCSB recommendations, the Secure Score, asset inventory and the default compliance view. A is wrong: Defender for Servers Plan 2 is a workload protection plan; it does not substitute for the Defender CSPM plan. B is wrong: attack path analysis has nothing to do with Defender XDR correlation.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: Contoso's VMs are on Defender for Servers Plan 1. The team expects to see agentless malware scanning, agentless secrets scanning, and file integrity monitoring for these VMs in Defender for Cloud, but none of them appear. Vulnerability results and EDR telemetry do appear. What is the gap?
options: Upgrade the VMs from Defender for Servers Plan 1 to Plan 2, which adds agentless scanning (malware, secrets), Defender Vulnerability Management premium features, and file integrity monitoring; Plan 1 already includes EDR and agent-based vulnerability scanning
Stay on Plan 1 and add a Sentinel analytics rule, because Plan 1 collects no telemetry at all and only the detection rule is missing
Enable Defender for Containers, because vulnerability assessment for VMs is bundled with the container plan
Enable just-in-time VM access, because it triggers agentless scanning whenever a JIT session opens
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Plan 1 is entry-level and focuses on the EDR capabilities from the Defender for Endpoint integration, and agent-based vulnerability scanning is included in both plans, so EDR and vulnerability results correctly appear. Agentless malware scanning, agentless secrets scanning, network-layer threat detection, MDVM premium features and file integrity monitoring are Plan 2 only. B is wrong: Plan 1 does collect EDR telemetry. C is wrong: the container plan does not cover VM agentless scanning. D is wrong: JIT access controls management ports; it does not trigger scanning.
questions.source_title: Select a Defender for Servers plan
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 2 provides the same features as Plan 1, and more: agentless scanning for machine posture scanning, vulnerability assessment, threat protection, malware scanning, and secrets scanning."

questions.question: Contoso's Defender for Cloud Secure Score is 78 percent and the team believes its posture is well covered. A penetration test finds a forgotten public subdomain with an expired certificate and an open management port, an asset nobody in IT knew existed. The CISO asks why a 78 percent score did not prevent this. What is the correct explanation?
options: The subdomain is not covered because attack path analysis only runs on Azure resources, and this host is on AWS
The subdomain is not a known resource in any connected cloud, so inside-out CSPM cannot see it; only outside-in EASM discovery, seeded with the company's domains, would have found it
The subdomain is not covered because Sentinel analytics rules were not enabled for DNS, which is the only way to find external assets
The subdomain is not covered because the Secure Score is too low, and raising the score would have discovered it
questions.explanation: Correct: B. EASM is the outside-in capability that discovers unknown internet-facing assets; Defender CSPM is inside-out and assesses only resources it already knows about in connected clouds, so it cannot see an undocumented subdomain. Attack path analysis operates on the cloud security graph of known resources. D is wrong: the score measures known-resource posture; raising it does not discover unknown assets. A is wrong: the miss is about unknown assets, not cloud provider. C is wrong: Sentinel rules are detections on ingested logs, not external discovery.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: A governance rule assigns a high-severity Defender for Cloud recommendation to a team with a 30-day deadline. The deadline passes and nobody acted. The CISO expects the recommendation to be auto-remediated or at least escalated by the rule, and the Secure Score to have dropped. What is the actual state?
options: The recommendation is removed from the list, because the governance rule marks it as accepted risk
The recommendation is automatically remediated when the deadline passes, and the Secure Score rises at that point

Nothing is fixed: a governance rule only assigns an owner and a deadline with reminders; actual remediation requires workflow automation, the Fix action, or manual work, and the score only changes when the configuration is actually remediated
The recommendation is escalated to the subscription owner, who is forced to remediate it before the deadline
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Governance rules assign owners and deadlines and send reminders; they are an accountability mechanism, not a remediation engine. Actual remediation comes from workflow automation (which triggers Logic Apps when recommendations are created or changed), the Fix button on a recommendation, or a Logic App. A governance rule's deadline does not execute anything, does not raise the Secure Score, and does not change the recommendation's state.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: Contoso must report compliance against NIST SP 800-53 for a federal customer, but the team does not want to lose the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark baseline. A colleague proposes removing the MCSB and replacing it with NIST, and another says all standards are free in Foundational CSPM. What is the correct approach?
options: Keep the MCSB, which cannot be removed, and add NIST SP 800-53; first enable at least one paid Defender for Cloud plan, since additional standards require one
Remove the MCSB and replace it with NIST SP 800-53, because only one standard can be assigned per subscription
Create a custom security standard named NIST SP 800-53, because Defender for Cloud has no built-in NIST mapping
Add NIST SP 800-53 in the Regulatory compliance dashboard at no cost, because all standards are free in Foundational CSPM
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The MCSB is the default standard, assigned automatically and not removable; additional standards such as NIST SP 800-53 can be added alongside it, but require at least one paid plan enabled in Defender for Cloud. B is wrong: standards are additive. C is wrong: NIST SP 800-53 is available as a built-in standard; inventing a custom one is unnecessary. D is wrong: only the MCSB compliance view is free; additional standards need a paid plan.
questions.source_title: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "When you turn on Defender for Cloud in a subscription, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) standard is applied by default in the subscription."

questions.question: Defender EASM flags an internet-exposed IP belonging to Contoso. The security team wants to know whether that exposure actually leads anywhere dangerous inside the environment, rather than just knowing the IP is exposed. Which Defender for Cloud capability uses EASM data to answer that, and what does it do?
options: The EASM finding automatically raises the Secure Score, because external exposure is an MCSB recommendation
The EASM finding automatically creates a Sentinel incident, because EASM is a Sentinel data connector
The EASM finding automatically enables Defender for Servers on the exposed host

The EASM data feeds attack path analysis in Defender CSPM, which finds exploitable paths starting from internet-exposed IPs, and cloud security explorer queries that correlate those IPs with Defender for Cloud data
questions.explanation: Correct: D. EASM findings feed into Defender CSPM's attack path analysis, which finds exploitable paths starting from internet-exposed IPs, and into cloud security explorer queries that correlate internet-exposed IPs with the rest of Defender for Cloud data. A is wrong: EASM does not raise the Secure Score (only MCSB recommendations do). B is wrong: EASM does not generate Sentinel incidents by itself. C is wrong: EASM does not add Defender for Servers protection; it is a discovery and exposure capability, not a protection plan.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: Contoso's board compares two numbers: the classic Secure Score in the Azure portal is 64 percent, while the new Cloud Secure Score in the Microsoft Defender portal is 41 percent for the same estate. A director insists one of them is broken. What is the correct explanation?
options: The Defender portal score is broken, because both scores use the same MCSB calculation and must match

The two scores are different models: the classic Secure Score is the MCSB-based score in the Azure portal, while the new Cloud Secure Score is a risk-based model in the Defender portal that incorporates asset risk factors and criticality, so the values legitimately differ
The Defender portal score only counts Preview recommendations, while the Azure portal score counts built-in ones
The scores differ because the Defender portal score is recalculated monthly and the Azure portal score every eight hours
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft Defender for Cloud now offers two Secure Score models: the classic Secure Score in the Azure portal and the new risk-based Cloud Secure Score in the Defender portal, which incorporates asset risk factors and criticality for more accurate prioritisation. They are completely different models with different calculations and values. A is wrong: the models are intentionally different. C reverses the Preview rule (Preview recommendations are excluded from the classic score). D invents a monthly cycle; classic controls are calculated every eight hours.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Only built-in recommendations from the MCSB affect the secure score."

questions.question: After remediating a recommendation, an engineer checks the Secure Score an hour later and sees no change, then checks the recommendation itself and sees the resource count has already dropped. The engineer concludes the score is frozen. What is happening?
options: The remediation did not work, because only the control-level count matters and recommendations never update
The score only updates when the Defender CSPM plan is enabled
The score is frozen until the next monthly recalculation

Recommendations within a control are updated more often than the control itself, and Defender for Cloud calculates each control every eight hours, so the recommendation count can move before the score does
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Recommendations within a control are updated more often than the control itself, and each control is calculated every eight hours for each subscription or cloud connector, so you can see discrepancies between the resource count on the recommendation and the resource count on the control. C is wrong: there is no monthly cycle. A is wrong: the recommendation count moving shows the remediation registered. B is wrong: the classic score exists in Foundational CSPM.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud calculates each control every eight hours for each Azure subscription or for each AWS or GCP cloud connector."

questions.question: Contoso has three subscriptions with Secure Scores of 40, 60 and 80 percent. The CISO reports a combined score of 60 percent as the average and is challenged by the auditor. What does Learn say about the combined score?
options: The combined score is the average of the subscription scores, so 60 percent is correct
The combined score is the lowest subscription score, so it should be 40 percent
The combined score is not an average; it is the evaluated posture of the status of all resources across all subscriptions and connectors
The combined score is the highest subscription score, so it should be 80 percent
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The combined score is not an average; rather, it is the evaluated posture of the status of all resources across all subscriptions and connectors. Averaging percentages would misrepresent the underlying resource counts. A, B and D each invent a combining rule Learn does not use.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Only built-in recommendations from the MCSB affect the secure score."

questions.question: A risk analyst enables risk prioritisation in Defender for Cloud and expects the classic Secure Score to jump, because the riskiest findings are now weighted. The score does not change. Is this expected?
options: No, risk prioritisation always changes the score because it reweights controls
Yes: currently, risk prioritization doesn't affect the secure score; the classic score is driven only by built-in MCSB recommendations
No, the score only changes if the Defender CSPM plan is enabled at the same time
Yes, but only because the score is capped at the value it had before risk prioritisation was enabled
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Learn states that currently, risk prioritisation doesn't affect the secure score; the classic score is driven only by built-in MCSB recommendations. A is wrong: prioritisation changes ordering and focus, not the classic score maths. C is wrong: the plan does not change this rule. D invents a cap.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Currently, risk prioritization doesn't affect the secure score."

questions.question: Contoso's cloud security explorer query finds an internet-exposed VM that has a critical vulnerability, holds a storage account key, and can reach a database containing customer data. The analyst wants to know which node to fix first to break the most attack paths. What concept should they use, and which plan feature provides these queries?
options: Fix the storage key first, because keys are always the choke point; this is a Defender for Servers Plan 1 feature
Fix the database first, because it is the final target; cloud security explorer is a Foundational CSPM feature
Fix the choke point, the node many attack paths pass through; cloud security explorer and attack path analysis are Defender CSPM plan features
Fix the VM's public IP first, because IP addresses are always the choke point; this is a Sentinel workbook feature
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Attack path analysis and cloud security explorer are Defender CSPM plan features that model exploitable paths on the cloud security graph; a choke point is a node many paths pass through, so fixing it breaks the most paths. B is wrong: the final target is not necessarily the best fix, and explorer queries are not in Foundational CSPM. D is wrong: the choke point depends on the graph, not on the IP, and this is not a Sentinel workbook. A is wrong: keys are not always the choke point, and this is not a Servers Plan 1 feature.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: A recommendation is marked healthy for a storage account, but the same storage account still appears in an attack path to a critical database. The engineer argues the attack path must be wrong. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The attack path is a Sentinel incident, not a Defender for Cloud finding, so it should be ignored here
The attack path is wrong, because a healthy recommendation means the resource is safe
Recommendations assess individual controls; attack paths model how multiple individually-acceptable weaknesses chain together, so a healthy single control does not make the path impossible
The attack path only appears when the Secure Score is below 50 percent, so the score must be wrong
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Recommendations assess individual controls against the benchmark, while attack path analysis models chains of exploitable steps across resources; several individually acceptable weaknesses can still combine into a viable path. B is wrong: healthy on one control does not mean safe in combination. D invents a score threshold. A is wrong: attack paths are a Defender for Cloud (Defender CSPM) capability, not Sentinel incidents.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: Contoso enables the Defender CSPM plan at the management group scope, expecting every subscription underneath to get attack path analysis. One subscription still shows no attack paths, and its owner says the plan was never enabled there. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Attack path analysis requires Defender for Servers Plan 2 on every VM in the subscription, not the CSPM plan
Attack path analysis is only available in the Azure portal, not the Defender portal
The subscription needs a Sentinel workspace before attack paths can be computed
Plans enabled at management group scope do not inherit to subscriptions; the plan must be enabled per subscription
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Defender for Cloud plans are enabled per subscription (or per management group with inheritance configured); if the subscription does not show the plan, it was not effectively enabled there, and the team should verify the plan state on that subscription. A is wrong: attack paths are a Defender CSPM feature, not a Servers feature. B is wrong: Defender for Cloud is expanding into the Defender portal and attack paths are a CSPM capability either way. C is wrong: Sentinel is not a prerequisite for attack path analysis.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: The SOC wants Defender for Cloud security alerts to appear in Sentinel automatically, and wants recommendations exported for long-term trending. A colleague proposes building a Logic App that scrapes the portal. What is the supported approach?
options: Enable workflow automation, which exports all historical recommendations to Sentinel on a schedule
Raise the Secure Score above 80 percent, which automatically enables the Sentinel export
Scrape the portal with a Logic App, because Defender for Cloud has no export mechanism
Use continuous export to stream Defender for Cloud alerts and recommendations to a Log Analytics workspace (and onward to Sentinel), or connect the Defender for Cloud data connector in Sentinel
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Defender for Cloud supports continuous export of alerts and recommendations to a Log Analytics workspace, Event Hub or storage, and Sentinel has a Defender for Cloud data connector; either route brings the data into Sentinel. C is wrong: scraping is unsupported and unnecessary. A is wrong: workflow automation triggers Logic Apps on new or changed recommendations/alerts; it is not a bulk historical export. B invents a score threshold.
questions.source_title: SC-500 study guide
questions.source_quote: "Manage security posture by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud."

questions.question: Contoso's workflow automation triggers a Logic App every time a recommendation changes state, but the team also wants an owner assigned and a due date set on the same recommendation. The engineer expects the workflow automation to do both. What is wrong with this expectation?
options: Nothing is wrong: workflow automation assigns owners and due dates as well as triggering Logic Apps
Workflow automation only triggers Logic Apps on recommendation or alert events; ownership and deadlines come from governance rules, which are a separate Defender CSPM feature
Workflow automation cannot trigger on recommendations at all; it only triggers on security alerts
Governance rules trigger Logic Apps, and workflow automation assigns owners; the engineer has the two features backwards
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Workflow automation triggers a Logic App when a recommendation or alert is created or changed; governance rules are the separate mechanism that assigns an owner, a due date and reminders. A conflates the two features. C is wrong: workflow automation does trigger on recommendations. D reverses the two features.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: Contoso onboards an on-premises Windows server fleet to Defender for Servers. The servers are not in Azure at all. An engineer says Defender for Servers cannot protect them because they are not Azure VMs. What is the correct onboarding path?
options: Install the Sentinel agent, which enrolls on-premises servers in Defender for Servers automatically
Enable Defender for Containers, which covers on-premises servers as container hosts
Defender for Servers cannot protect non-Azure machines under any plan
Onboard the servers through Azure Arc, which extends Defender for Cloud protection to hybrid machines, including vulnerability assessment and EDR via the Defender for Endpoint integration
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Defender for Servers protects VMs on Azure, AWS and GCP and on-premises machines connected through Azure Arc; Arc onboarding brings the machines into Defender for Cloud so the Servers plan, including the Defender for Endpoint integration, applies. C is wrong: hybrid support is a documented Servers capability. A is wrong: the Sentinel agent does not enroll servers in Defender for Servers. B is wrong: the container plan protects container workloads, not general on-premises servers.
questions.source_title: Overview of Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 1 is entry-level, and focuses on the EDR capabilities provided by the Defender for Endpoint integration."

questions.question: A VM in Azure has Defender for Servers Plan 2 enabled, and the team sees agentless vulnerability results within hours of onboarding, with no agent installed on the VM. A colleague insists an agent must have been installed silently. What is the correct explanation?
options: Agentless scanning only works for AWS VMs, so this Azure result must be from the Defender for Endpoint agent
Agentless scanning is a Sentinel feature, not a Defender for Servers feature
An agent was installed silently, because vulnerability scanning always requires an agent

Defender for Servers Plan 2 provides agentless machine scanning: without an agent on endpoints, you can scan software inventory, assess machines for vulnerabilities, scan for machine secrets, and detect malware threats
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Plan 2 provides agentless scanning, enabled by default when you enable Defender for Servers Plan 2; it scans software inventory, assesses vulnerabilities, scans for machine secrets and detects malware without an agent. C is wrong: agentless scanning is explicitly agent-free. A is wrong: agentless scanning covers Azure, AWS and GCP. B is wrong: this is a Defender for Servers Plan 2 capability.
questions.source_title: Overview of Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 1 is entry-level, and focuses on the EDR capabilities provided by the Defender for Endpoint integration."

questions.question: Contoso's EASM inventory shows a subdomain pointing at an IP range the company sold two years ago. The team wants EASM to stop tracking it, but the asset keeps reappearing in the inventory. What is the most likely cause, and what should they check first?
options: EASM never removes assets, so the inventory is permanent and must be ignored
The seed inputs still include the old domain or IP range, so EASM keeps rediscovering related assets; review and remove stale seeds (domains, IP ranges, ASNs) from the EASM configuration
The asset reappears because the Secure Score is below 70 percent; raise the score to clear it
EASM only discovers Azure resources, so a sold IP range cannot be in the inventory at all
questions.explanation: Correct: B. EASM discovery starts from seed inputs such as known domains, IP ranges and ASNs and continuously discovers related assets; a stale seed keeps the sold range in scope. A is wrong: EASM inventory reflects its seeds and discovered connections, and stale seeds can be removed. C invents a score rule. D is wrong: EASM is outside-in and discovers internet-facing assets regardless of cloud provider.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: Contoso enables Defender for SQL on its Azure SQL databases. The team expects vulnerability assessment findings for the databases to appear, but only threat detection alerts appear. What is missing?
options: Vulnerability assessment for SQL is included in Defender for Servers Plan 1, so enable that on the database
Vulnerability assessment only runs when the Secure Score exceeds 80 percent
Sentinel must be enabled first, because SQL vulnerability assessment is a Sentinel analytics rule

Defender for SQL threat detection and vulnerability assessment are separate capabilities: enable the vulnerability assessment feature for the databases (with a storage account for scan results) alongside the threat detection plan
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Defender for SQL provides advanced threat protection (anomalous access, SQL injection attempts) as a workload plan, while vulnerability assessment is a separate SQL capability that discovers and remediates database vulnerabilities and stores scan results; both must be configured. A is wrong: Defender for Servers protects machines, not Azure SQL databases. B invents a score threshold. C is wrong: SQL vulnerability assessment is a Defender/SQL feature, not a Sentinel rule.
questions.source_title: SC-500 study guide
questions.source_quote: "Manage security posture by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud."

questions.question: Contoso enables Defender for Storage and expects every blob upload to be scanned for malware in near real time. Uploads of large archives take noticeably longer to become available, and the team asks whether scanning is blocking the upload. How does Defender for Storage malware scanning work, and what should they expect?
options: Malware scanning only applies to files already in the account before the plan was enabled
Defender for Storage malware scanning requires Sentinel to be enabled, otherwise no scanning happens at all

Malware scanning in Defender for Storage scans blobs on upload in near real time and can block or tag malicious content; large files take longer to scan, so availability can be delayed while scanning completes
Defender for Storage only scans blobs once a week on a schedule, so uploads are never delayed
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Defender for Storage includes malware scanning on upload (near real time) as part of the workload plan; scanning inspects content as it arrives, so large files can take longer before they are available. D is wrong: scanning is on-upload, not weekly. A is wrong: scanning applies to new uploads, not only pre-existing blobs. B is wrong: Sentinel is not a prerequisite for Defender for Storage scanning.
questions.source_title: SC-500 study guide
questions.source_quote: "Manage security posture by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud."

questions.question: A developer proposes storing a storage account access key in a VM's environment variables so an app can reach the account, and asks Defender for Cloud to approve it. The cloud security explorer already flags the key as exposed on the VM. What is the secure alternative, and why does the explorer flag this?
options: Use a managed identity for the VM (or workload identity) so the app authenticates without a stored secret; the explorer flags the key because an internet-exposed VM holding a key creates an exploitable attack path to the storage account
Move the key into the Secure Score, because the score stores secrets securely
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 1, which encrypts environment variables automatically
Keep the key in environment variables, because Defender for Cloud approves keys stored outside the codebase
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Managed identities let Azure resources authenticate without stored credentials, removing the secret from the VM entirely; cloud security explorer flags the exposed key because it is a node on an attack path from the internet-exposed VM to the storage account. D is wrong: environment variables are not a secure secret store. B is wrong: the Secure Score is a posture metric, not a secret store. C is wrong: no Defender plan encrypts environment variables.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: Contoso's just-in-time (JIT) VM access policy closes RDP and SSH ports by default. An administrator opens a JIT session to patch a VM, and during the session a vulnerability scan reports the management ports as open. The administrator concludes JIT is broken. What is the correct interpretation?
options: JIT is working as designed: it opens the requested management port for a limited time window to the requesting source, then closes it again; the scan observed the port during the approved window
JIT only works on VMs without Defender for Servers enabled, so the scan result proves the plan is misconfigured
JIT opens ports permanently once used, so the port will stay open until the VM is rebuilt
JIT is broken, because ports must never appear open during a session
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Just-in-time VM access reduces the attack surface by keeping management ports closed by default and opening them only for an approved, time-limited session from a specific source; a scan during that window correctly sees the port open. D is wrong: the open state during the window is the intended behaviour. B is wrong: JIT is a Defender for Servers feature, not something that conflicts with it. C is wrong: JIT sessions expire and the port closes automatically.
questions.source_title: Overview of Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 1 is entry-level, and focuses on the EDR capabilities provided by the Defender for Endpoint integration."

questions.question: Contoso's Defender for Cloud shows a recommendation to enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration on a set of VMs, but the VMs already show EDR alerts in the Defender portal. The team debates whether the recommendation is stale. What should they check?
options: Raise the Secure Score, because recommendations disappear automatically above 90 percent
Ignore the recommendation, because EDR alerts prove the integration is already enabled on those VMs

Check whether the recommendation targets a different scope (for example, a specific subscription, resource group, or machine set) or a different integration setting, because recommendations are scoped and the alerts may come from machines where the integration is enabled
Disable Defender for Endpoint, because the recommendation and the alerts cannot both be correct
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Recommendations are scoped to subscriptions, resource groups and resources; EDR alerts in the portal may come from machines where the integration is enabled, while the recommendation flags machines or scopes where it is not. B is wrong: alerts from some machines do not prove the integration is enabled everywhere. D is wrong: disabling EDR would remove protection. A invents a score rule.
questions.source_title: Overview of Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 1 is entry-level, and focuses on the EDR capabilities provided by the Defender for Endpoint integration."

questions.question: A new subscription shows a Secure Score of 100 percent on day one, before the team has hardened anything. The CISO is suspicious. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Foundational CSPM gives every new subscription a free 100 percent for the first 30 days
The score is wrong, because a new subscription always starts at 0 percent

The score reflects only the resources currently in scope against the MCSB controls; a nearly empty subscription with few assessable resources can score highly, and the score will fall as more (unhardened) resources are added
The score starts at 100 percent for every subscription and only decreases, so it is meaningless
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The Secure Score aggregates findings for resources in scope against MCSB controls; with almost no resources in scope there are few findings to deduct, so an empty subscription can score highly. The score is meaningful as resources are added and assessed. B is wrong: there is no fixed starting score. D is wrong: the score is recalculated from real assessments, not a countdown. A invents a 30-day free period.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Only built-in recommendations from the MCSB affect the secure score."

questions.question: Contoso's compliance team wants the Regulatory compliance dashboard to show a custom internal control framework that is not PCI DSS, ISO 27001 or NIST. The team proposes naming a recommendation after the framework. What is the correct approach?
options: Assign a built-in security standard that maps to the framework's controls where one exists, and use Azure Policy initiatives to assess the remaining custom controls; Defender for Cloud evaluates standards as collections of controls backed by assessments, not by renaming recommendations
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2, which creates custom standards automatically from recommendation names
Remove the MCSB and replace it with the custom framework, because only one standard can be assigned
Name a recommendation after the framework, because Defender for Cloud lets any recommendation define a new standard
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Security standards in Defender for Cloud are collections of controls evaluated through assessments (backed by Azure Policy initiatives); where no built-in standard matches, the team should use the closest built-in standard and cover the rest with Azure Policy. D is wrong: renaming a recommendation does not create a standard. B is wrong: workload plans do not create standards. C is wrong: the MCSB cannot be removed and standards are additive.
questions.source_title: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "When you turn on Defender for Cloud in a subscription, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) standard is applied by default in the subscription."

questions.question: Contoso connects an AWS account to Defender for Cloud. The AWS posture appears, but no Defender for Servers protection is available for the EC2 instances. What is the most likely gap?
options: AWS instances are protected automatically by Foundational CSPM, so the team must be looking at the wrong portal
Defender for Servers only protects GCP instances, not AWS
Defender for Cloud does not support AWS at all, so the posture view must be from another tool

The cloud connector provides posture (CSPM) for the AWS account, but workload protection for EC2 instances requires enabling the Defender for Servers plan and onboarding the instances (via the connector/Arc agent path) so the plan applies to them
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Connecting an AWS account with a cloud connector brings its posture into Defender for Cloud, but protecting EC2 instances needs the Defender for Servers plan enabled and the machines onboarded so the plan's agent/EDR integration applies. C is wrong: AWS posture is supported. A is wrong: Foundational CSPM is posture assessment, not workload protection. B is wrong: Defender for Servers supports Azure, AWS and GCP machines.
questions.source_title: Overview of Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 1 is entry-level, and focuses on the EDR capabilities provided by the Defender for Endpoint integration."

questions.question: A Defender for Cloud recommendation says 'Machines should have a vulnerability assessment solution'. The VM already has the Defender for Endpoint agent and shows vulnerability results. The engineer wants to exempt the VM. What should they do first?
options: Delete the VM, because a recommendation that cannot be remediated means the resource is non-compliant by design
Enable Sentinel, because only Sentinel can clear Defender for Cloud recommendations
Exempt it immediately, because the agent proves the recommendation is wrong

Verify which assessment the recommendation refers to (agent-based MDVM via the Endpoint agent versus agentless scanning) and whether the VM is in scope for the plan that provides it, before exempting; an exemption hides the finding without fixing a real gap
questions.explanation: Correct: D. The recommendation can refer to a specific assessment path (agent-based MDVM or Plan 2 agentless scanning); the team should confirm which one is missing and whether the VM is in the plan's scope before exempting, since exemptions suppress the finding. C is wrong: the agent's presence does not prove the specific assessment the recommendation checks is in place. A is wrong: deletion is not a remediation strategy. B is wrong: Sentinel does not clear Defender recommendations.
questions.source_title: Overview of Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 1 is entry-level, and focuses on the EDR capabilities provided by the Defender for Endpoint integration."

questions.question: Contoso's EASM data shows an internet-facing test server with a critical vulnerability, and the same server appears as the entry point of three different attack paths to three critical assets. The team has one maintenance window and can fix only one thing. What should they prioritise, and why?
options: Fix the database, because it is the final target of all three paths
Fix the test server (or remove its internet exposure), because it is the choke point the three paths share; removing the shared entry point breaks all three paths at once
Fix the Secure Score, because the score is the root cause of the attack paths
Fix the Sentinel analytics rule, because attack paths are created by analytics rules
questions.explanation: Correct: B. When one node sits on multiple attack paths it is a choke point; fixing or removing the shared entry point breaks all the paths that depend on it, which is the highest-leverage single fix. A is wrong: hardening one target leaves the other two paths intact. C is wrong: the score measures posture; it does not cause paths. D is wrong: attack paths come from the cloud security graph, not Sentinel rules.
questions.source_title: External attack surface management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Attack path analysis helps you to address the security issues that pose immediate threats with the greatest potential of being exploited in your environment."

questions.question: Contoso disables a Defender for Cloud recommendation's underlying Azure Policy initiative, expecting the recommendation to disappear. It remains, now showing as not applicable for some resources. What happened?
options: Recommendations are driven by assessments; disabling the backing initiative stops new assessments, but existing assessment state can linger until the next evaluation cycle, and resources outside the initiative's scope show as not applicable
Recommendations are independent of Azure Policy, so disabling the initiative has no effect at all
The recommendation can only be removed by raising the Secure Score to 100 percent
Disabling the initiative deletes the recommendation immediately, so the team must be looking at a cached page
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Many Defender for Cloud recommendations are backed by Azure Policy initiatives that perform the assessment; changing the initiative affects future evaluations, and state can persist until the next cycle, while out-of-scope resources report as not applicable. D is wrong: there is no immediate deletion. B is wrong: standards and recommendations are backed by policy initiatives and assessments. C invents a score rule.
questions.source_title: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "When you turn on Defender for Cloud in a subscription, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) standard is applied by default in the subscription."

questions.question: Contoso's Defender for Cloud shows a high-severity recommendation for a storage account that the team remediated yesterday by enabling the required setting. The recommendation still shows as unhealthy. The engineer concludes the remediation failed. What should they check first?
options: Whether the storage account was deleted, because only deletion clears a recommendation

Whether the assessment has re-run since the change: Defender for Cloud calculates each control every eight hours, so a fix can take up to a cycle to reflect, and recommendations update more often than controls
Whether the Secure Score is above 90 percent, because recommendations only refresh above that threshold
Whether Sentinel is enabled, because recommendations only refresh when Sentinel ingests the change
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Controls are calculated every eight hours and recommendations update on their own cycle, so a remediation made yesterday may not yet be reflected; the team should wait for the next evaluation and then re-check. C invents a score threshold. D is wrong: Sentinel is not involved in Defender recommendation refresh. A is wrong: deletion is not the way recommendations clear.
questions.source_title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud calculates each control every eight hours for each Azure subscription or for each AWS or GCP cloud connector."

questions.question: Contoso wants data-aware security posture: to know which cloud storage resources hold sensitive data, so attack paths to those resources can be prioritised. Which Defender CSPM capability provides this, and what does it need?
options: Defender for Storage malware scanning, which classifies data by sensitivity as it scans for malware
The Secure Score, which lists every file containing sensitive data

Data-aware security posture in the Defender CSPM plan, which discovers sensitive data in cloud resources so exposure of sensitive data can be prioritised in attack paths; it requires the Defender CSPM plan
Foundational CSPM, which classifies all sensitive data in every storage account for free
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Data-aware security posture is a Defender CSPM plan capability that identifies sensitive data in cloud resources, letting the team prioritise attack paths that lead to sensitive data. D is wrong: sensitive-data discovery is not a free Foundational CSPM feature. A is wrong: malware scanning detects malicious content, not data sensitivity. B is wrong: the Secure Score is an aggregate number, not a data inventory.
questions.source_title: Cloud security posture management in Defender for Cloud
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Cloud includes free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Enable advanced CSPM capabilities by using the Defender CSPM plan."

questions.question: A security alert fires in Defender for Cloud for a VM: 'Suspicious process executed'. A recommendation for the same VM says 'Enable EDR'. The analyst treats the alert and the recommendation as the same thing and closes the recommendation to clear the alert. What is wrong with this?
options: Recommendations are reactive detections and alerts are proactive findings, so the analyst had them backwards but the action was still correct
Nothing is wrong: closing a recommendation clears its alerts

Alerts and recommendations are different: an alert is a reactive detection of a specific suspicious event that needs investigation, while a recommendation is a proactive posture finding about a missing control; closing the recommendation does not investigate or clear the alert
Alerts are only created by Sentinel, so this alert must be a Sentinel incident, not a Defender for Cloud alert
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Alerts are detections of active suspicious activity requiring triage and investigation; recommendations are posture findings about configuration gaps. They are managed separately, and closing a recommendation does not resolve an alert. B is wrong: the two are not linked that way. D is wrong: Defender for Cloud workload plans generate their own security alerts. A reverses the definitions and the action was not correct.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview
questions.source_quote: "Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a Cloud Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), which is a unified solution that combines multiple cloud security tools to protect applications across their entire lifecycle."

questions.question: Contoso's Defender for Servers Plan 2 VMs show file integrity monitoring (FIM) findings for unexpected changes to system files. A colleague says FIM is included in Plan 1 and the team overpaid. Is that correct?
options: Yes, FIM is in both plans, so Plan 2 was unnecessary for FIM alone
No: file integrity monitoring to examine files and registries for changes that might indicate an attack is a Plan 2 capability, alongside agentless scanning and MDVM premium features
No, FIM is a Sentinel feature and is not part of either Servers plan
Yes, but only for Linux VMs; Windows VMs need Plan 2 for FIM
questions.explanation: Correct: B. File integrity monitoring, which examines files and registries for changes that might indicate an attack, is listed among the additional capabilities of Defender for Servers Plan 2, together with agentless scanning and premium Defender Vulnerability Management features. A is wrong: Plan 1 focuses on EDR via the Defender for Endpoint integration. C is wrong: FIM here is a Defender for Servers capability. D invents an OS split.
questions.source_title: Select a Defender for Servers plan
questions.source_quote: "Defender for Servers Plan 2 provides the same features as Plan 1, and more: agentless scanning for machine posture scanning, vulnerability assessment, threat protection, malware scanning, and secrets scanning."

questions.question: Contoso's CISO asks for a single view that combines Defender for Cloud posture, Defender XDR incidents, and Sentinel detections for the same estate. A colleague says the three products cannot be viewed together. What is the correct answer?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is expanding into the Defender portal to provide a unified security experience, and Sentinel onboarded to the Defender portal shares the unified incident queue with Defender XDR, so posture, incidents and detections can be worked in one place
Only Sentinel can show all three, because Defender for Cloud and Defender XDR have no portal integration
The unified view requires deleting the Sentinel workspace and recreating it in the Defender portal
They cannot be combined; each product must be used in its own portal
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Defender for Cloud is expanding to the Defender portal for a unified security experience, and Sentinel onboarded to the Defender portal triages incidents in the unified queue alongside Defender XDR, so posture and detection data converge in one portal. D is wrong: unification is the direction of the platform. B is wrong: the Defender portal is the unified surface, not Sentinel alone. C is wrong: onboarding connects the existing workspace; it does not require deleting it.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview
questions.source_quote: "Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a Cloud Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), which is a unified solution that combines multiple cloud security tools to protect applications across their entire lifecycle."
